name: Halftime to Final Total
summary: Set the halftime numbers for both teams and get the expected final combined score, with a range.

synopsis_extra: With {floor} points already on the board, that means about {remaining} more in the second half.

card.holdout_label: 2025 season onward (422 games the model never saw)
findings: Two things carry almost all of the signal: the halftime score and the pregame over/under. A point already on the board is worth about 0.99 points in the final total, so first-half scoring neither snowballs nor fades much. Each point of the pregame over/under adds about 0.38.

Moving the ball without scoring still counts a little: each first down adds about 0.15 points and each 20+ yard play adds about 0.23. Offenses that looked better than the scoreboard tend to cash in later.
Wind is the only weather input that held up. Every 10 mph takes about 0.8 points off the final total.
Lopsided games slow down. Each point of halftime margin trims about 0.08 points, so a 21-point lead costs roughly 1.6 as the leader runs the clock.

Tested and left out because they added nothing once the score and the betting line were known: turnovers, third-down conversion rate, penalties, red-zone trips, how pass-heavy each team was, punts, field goal tries, sacks, total yards, play counts, the point spread, dome or outdoors, grass or turf, temperature, who gets the second-half kickoff, each team's season scoring average. Most of what these stats tell you already shows up in the score.
Advanced stats (EPA per play, success rate, shotgun and no-huddle share) were also tried. They did not beat plain box-score stats (9.64 vs 9.63 points of typical error), so the inputs stay simple.

Honest scorecard: on games it never saw, the model misses by 7.6 points on average. That is far better than doubling the halftime score (10.0) or using the pregame over/under alone (10.5), but only about 0.1 points of error better than the simple recipe of halftime score plus half the over/under.
limitations: It only knows what you enter. Injuries, a quarterback change or a team sitting starters are invisible to it.
It is a straight-line model, so it cannot capture special situations such as a team that abandons the run when trailing big.
Overtime games are included in the history, which stretches the top of the range slightly.
The range is wide because second halves are noisy, and no halftime stat tested here narrows it much.
Sliders move independently, so you can enter combinations that rarely happen in real games. Unusual inputs are flagged.
card.disclaimer: For information and learning only. Not betting advice.
